name: The ear on the north brow
text: There's a great black dish of Builders' stone on the brow of the north shore turned to face the city, and if you put your ear to the cup in front of it you can hear Tollmere talking, every word, as if it was at your elbow. A Quiet Hands woman sits there all day selling what she hears. They say if you listen long enough you hear something under the water too.
variants: Mind what you say on the Row on a still day. The Builders' ear on the north shore hears it, and so does Mab Larrow.

name: Rope with no heart
text: Every rope the Charter buys has a red yarn twisted into its heart, so a stolen fathom can be known by cutting it. Old Tarr at the Ropewalk has put it in for forty years. Somebody's asked him for sixty fathom without, and paid in salt with no seal on the sack.
variants: Walk the top home on the Ropewalk on the south shore and Tarr cuts you a fathom off it for luck. Red in the heart, as always.

name: The drowned-board
text: Out past Willow Isle on the south-west shingle there are three boats turned keel-up for houses, and a board by the water chalked with every boat lost off that shore since the Charter. Grisel Mew goes over the names every evening. Her own son's is the newest, and Hesper Kettle's boy swears he saw that boat tied up behind the Saltmound in the dark.
variants: Buy your smoked eel at the Widows' Keels, not on the Row. Cheaper, and the old woman says thank you.

name: Four stone light
text: The Charter Scale's still standing on the south shore by the Stride's Foot, the great beam that weighed every boat that came to Tollmere, and Prudence Gauge still keeps it true. She says the salt barges come down four stone light, every one of them, and the Saltmound's seals were never broken. A Weighmaster who can't make a sum come out is a Weighmaster who won't sleep.
variants: Bring the Charter Scale's beam level with the iron weights and the Weighmaster puts your name in her ledger as somebody who can count.

name: Birds named after taxes
text: Corbin Vell fishes with cormorants off the south-east shore, fourteen of them, all named after taxes. They bring up pike and rings and Tallymen's seals off the bottom. And at dusk some of them fly across the water to the city with something tied to their legs, and nobody on the Stride ever looks twice at a cormorant.

name: Eyes over the water
text: On an east wind you can see eyes hanging over the Mere from the Stride: kites, painted with staring eyes, flown off the east shingle below the Wold Water's mouth to carry baited lines out to the deep pike. A girl of eleven flies them for her mother, who's in the Undercroft for nineteen marks. She'll let you take a turn on a reel for half of what bites.

name: The fair where nobody speaks
text: There's a fair every night on the south-east shore inside a ring of black screens, and nothing in it is said aloud. Salt with no seal, rope with no red, Hush sayings in jars. You pay in knocks. The Tallymen know where it is. Everybody knows where it is. Nobody has ever heard it.
variants: If you go to the Dumb Fair, keep your mouth shut. The Hush-wife will put a finger on your lips the first time. There isn't a second time.

name: The King of Salt
text: You'll have seen the Saltmound white on the west shore, the Charter's tithe-salt heaped under seal. Old Marrow the salt-reeve swears his seals are whole, and they are. But there are boats at the back of it at night, toward the water, and a man who calls himself the Salt-King, and Gullhithe's poorest are paid in salt.
variants: Every barge out of the Saltmound weighs four stone light at the Charter Scale. Every barge. Somebody's counting.

name: The Patience came up empty
text: The Fathom Company's bell went down off the west tail three weeks ago with Master Lisle and four men after the Undersong, the drowned bell in the Quarter under the Mere, and came up with nobody in it, ringing. It's rung by itself every hour since. His daughter keeps the windlass and won't let anyone take the chain off it.
variants: They say the Drowned Quarter under the Mere is dry, forty fathom down; the water stops at its doors. The salvors go down in a bell and walk its streets.
